generatedProse.concept-context: A psychology presentation that delivers well has a structure the audience can follow: an introduction that frames the question or study, a main body that develops the argument in order, and a conclusion that leaves one clear message. Visual aids support that structure rather than replace it. A single clear graph of a result lands faster than a paragraph of text, but a slide crammed with method detail splits the audience between you and the screen. The slides prompt; you deliver.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students present on the same study, with the same findings to share.

Tom builds the slides first and lets them set the order. Each slide is full of text and method detail, and the talk becomes a reading of the screen. The talk has no clear opening or close, so the audience is unsure what the main finding means, and the slides pull their eyes away from Tom rather than supporting the argument. The material is all there, but it does not land.

Amara plans the structure first: an introduction that frames the research question, a main body of three ordered points, and a conclusion with one clear message about what the study shows. Only then do the slides follow, each one a prompt or a single clear graph. The audience can follow the argument, and the visual aids help it along. The delivery feels in control.

Both had the same findings. Only Amara let a structure lead and made the visual aids serve it.
generatedProse.summary: A psychology presentation delivers well when a clear structure leads it and the visual aids serve that structure. An introduction, an ordered main body and a conclusion give the audience a path through the study, and slides that prompt rather than script keep their attention on you. You can now build a supporting structure and design visual aids that back your argument. The final lesson looks at the errors that undo good preparation.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara's visual aids work better than Tom's?

items.text: They supported each point as prompts or a single clear graph, rather than carrying dense text.
They used brighter colours and more animation.
There were more slides, so the audience saw more.
They were written out in full so she could read them aloud.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara's visual aids supported each point as prompts or a clear graph, rather than carrying the talk.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what the visual aids were doing, not how they looked.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's visual aids worked because they prompted and supported each point. Colour, more slides or full text are not what made them effective.
